name: Selective amnesia
statement: Selective amnesia is the clinical name for recalling some but not all of a traumatic episode, and the everyday name for forgetting whatever is inconvenient.
meaning: Those are two different claims and only one of them is a diagnosis. In clinical use selective amnesia is one of the shapes a case of dissociative amnesia can take. David Spiegel's Merck Manual article defines it as 'forgetting some, but not all, of the events within a certain time period, or forgetting only part of a traumatic event'. It sets that beside localised amnesia for a whole period, generalised amnesia for identity and life history, systematised amnesia for one category of information such as everything about a particular person, and continuous amnesia for each new event as it occurs. Mangiulli, Otgaar, Jelicic and Merckelbach, reading DSM-5 at page 298, describe three forms rather than five, and report that localised amnesia is assumed there to be the most prevalent. The label describes the pattern of what is missing. It names no mechanism, and on its own it is not a diagnosis. The everyday sense is an accusation. It says somebody forgets on cue whatever is unflattering, and it supplies a motive the clinical term does not. This page is about the clinical term. What the search for the everyday sense as a measured claim returned is recorded below.

origin.where: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition
origin.note: The year is the publication year of the manual whose wording current clinical references use. DSM-5 itself was not obtained here. Its definition of dissociative amnesia is quoted through Mangiulli and colleagues, who cite page 298, and its subtypes through Spiegel's Merck Manual article. The phrase is older than DSM-5 and no source dating its first use was located. The earliest dated use found in this search is Hilgard and Hommel's 1961 paper in the Journal of Personality on selective amnesia for events within hypnosis, known here from its Crossref record and its title only.

evidence: The clinical evidence is case reports, and one review has counted them. Mangiulli, Otgaar, Jelicic and Merckelbach examined 128 cases of dissociative amnesia published in 60 English-language peer-reviewed articles between 2000 and 2020. Of the 128 patients, 60.9% were men, ages ran from 11 to 66, and 80.5% of the cases were clinical rather than forensic. The sample runs against what the manual leads a reader to expect. Memory loss covered extended lifetime periods in 75% of cases and circumscribed autobiographical events in 24.2%, where DSM-5 treats the circumscribed pattern as the common one. Two case studies out of 128 addressed every DSM-5 feature. The reviewers argue that both still had a plausible alternative account, transient global amnesia in one and malingering in the other. Ordinary forgetting was raised as an alternative explanation in two of the 31 cases with circumscribed memory loss, and encoding failure in three. Malingering was considered in 31.3% of all cases, and a forensic examination followed in 18 of those 40. Their conclusion is that as a diagnostic label dissociative amnesia is often prematurely used, and that no case study has yet met the DSM-5 bar convincingly. Prevalence is unsettled and the two secondary sources read here disagree at the bottom of the range. Spiegel gives general-population estimates of 0.2% to 7.3%, citing Staniloiu and Markowitsch's review and a 2006 community study. Mangiulli and colleagues give 1.8% to 7.3%, citing Spiegel and seven co-authors on the dissociative disorders in DSM-5, and Staniloiu and Markowitsch again. Neither of those cited papers was obtained. Two laboratory programmes carry the phrase without carrying the clinical claim. Clemes built word lists half of which were complex indicators drawn from each participant's own word-association latencies, had hypnotised participants learn them, then suggested partial amnesia. Kihlstrom and Hoyt report that recall favoured the neutral items, that a control group studying the list awake showed no differential recall, and that a later replication attempt by Stam, Radtke-Bodorik and Spanos failed, leaving the evidence equivocal. The second programme is mnemic neglect, whose flagship review by Sedikides, Green, Saunders, Skowronski and Zengel is subtitled 'Selective amnesia of one's faults'. It defines the effect as inferior recall for self-threatening feedback compared with other kinds of feedback. Participants take a bogus personality test, the Michigan Omnibus Personality Inventory, then read behaviours said to describe either themselves or a person called Chris. Liu, Deng and Yang's meta-analysis of 18 studies and 93 independent samples, N = 4,989, puts the effect at g = 0.365, 95% CI [0.253, 0.476], Z = 6.416, p < .001.

replication.headline: Nothing was found to replicate. Selective amnesia is a descriptor of a diagnosis rather than an experimental effect, and its case-report base is thin: of 128 published cases of dissociative amnesia, two addressed every DSM-5 feature and both had an ordinary explanation available.
replication.detail: A replication needs an effect with a procedure attached, and the clinical term has neither. It is a coding applied to a patient's reported pattern of memory loss. Mangiulli and colleagues used that coding as one variable in their scheme, and the breakdown of their 128 cases into localised, selective and generalised sits in a supplemental table that was not obtained, so no count of selective cases is quoted here. Searching for the phrase as the name of a measured effect returns work on other things. Europe PMC holds 102 records containing it and 10 whose titles carry it, and those 10 are limbic encephalitis, reversible hippocampal lesions, scopolamine in mice, quinolinic acid lesions in rat entorhinal cortex, suicide attempts, transient amnesia for merchandise prices, hypnotic suggestion, two pieces of medical humour and rhetoric, and Hilgard and Hommel's 1961 hypnosis paper. PubMed returns the same count of 10 for the phrase in a title. Neither list contains a study of forgetting part of a traumatic event, and neither contains a study of convenient forgetting. The two measured neighbours described above are not replications of this. Clemes and Stam concern hypnotic amnesia for conflict-linked words, and mnemic neglect concerns recall of trait feedback minutes after reading it. The clinical dispute meanwhile is live and is being conducted in commentary rather than in data. Otgaar, Howe, Patihis, Mangiulli, Dodier, Huntjens, Krackow, Jelicic and Lynn published a critique of the neuroscience of dissociative amnesia and repressed memory in Legal and Criminological Psychology in March 2025, and the same supplement carries three replies, one of them from Markowitsch and Staniloiu. Wiley returned 403 for all four, so they are recorded here from their Crossref records and titles alone.

limits: The search ran across Europe PMC by phrase and by title, PubMed by title, Crossref by bibliographic query, Semantic Scholar, and general web search. Only the English phrase was searched. DSM-5 was not obtained, so every statement about its text here is quoted through Mangiulli and colleagues or through Spiegel's Merck Manual article, and the difference between their two accounts of how many subtypes the manual lists is left standing rather than resolved. Wiley returned 403 for the 2025 Legal and Criminological Psychology exchange and for one of its commentaries, and Southampton's repository returned 403 for the Sedikides record, so the review was read instead as the accepted manuscript posted at Strathclyde. Clemes 1964 and Stam, Radtke-Bodorik and Spanos 1980 were not obtained; both are described here through Kihlstrom and Hoyt's 1990 chapter, and their bibliographic details come from Crossref and PubMed. Crossref records the 1964 author as Stanley Clemens while PubMed and every citing source seen here give Clemes, so the surname in that record is wrong. Cima, Merckelbach, Hollnack and Knauer's prison study was not obtained and its figure below is quoted through Mangiulli. Liu, Deng and Yang's meta-analysis was read in abstract only, so nothing is said here about which studies it pooled or how it handled publication bias. Mangiulli and colleagues state their own main limitation, that they reviewed case studies and left aside the experimental literature on amnesia-like phenomena, and that a review restricted to English peer-reviewed journals may have missed better-documented cases in other languages.
misreadings: The first error comes from the encyclopedia article a reader will meet first. Wikipedia files selective amnesia under memory biases, and its body is about electroconvulsive shock in rats, quinolinic acid lesions in rat entorhinal cortex, scopolamine in mice, hypnotic amnesia, and two patients with brain damage. None of that is the DSM-5 descriptor and none of it is convenient forgetting. The second error is to read a claim of selective amnesia as proof that something happened. It is a self-report, and it arrives most often where it pays. Cima and colleagues found that 72 of 308 forensic psychiatric inpatients, 23%, claimed total or partial amnesia for their crimes, a figure quoted here through Mangiulli's description of that study. In more than two thirds of the 128 reviewed cases the authors did not consider malingering at all. The third error is to hear the word selective as an accusation. In the clinical sense it describes which parts of an episode are missing, and it carries no claim that the patient chose. The fourth is to borrow the numbers from mnemic neglect. Its g of 0.365 is about how much trait feedback about oneself is written down at recall a few minutes later, which is not autobiographical memory loss for an event. This atlas covers the deliberate suppression of a memory when its cue returns under motivated forgetting, and that entry's think/no-think evidence does not transfer here either.

sources.text: Mangiulli, I., Otgaar, H., Jelicic, M., & Merckelbach, H. (2022). A Critical Review of Case Studies on Dissociative Amnesia. Clinical Psychological Science, 10(2), 191-211. Read in full as the PDF posted by the fourth author; the source for every figure in the first paragraph of the evidence section.

Spiegel, D. Dissociative Amnesia. Merck Manual Professional Edition, reviewed and revised June 2025. Read in full and fetched twice; the source for the five subtypes and for the 0.2% to 7.3% prevalence range.

Sedikides, C., Green, J. D., Saunders, J., Skowronski, J. J., & Zengel, B. (2016). Mnemic neglect: Selective amnesia of one's faults. European Review of Social Psychology, 27(1), 1-62. Accepted manuscript read in full at the Strathclyde repository; the source for the definition of the effect and for the Michigan Omnibus Personality Inventory procedure.

Liu, W., Deng, L., & Yang, H. (2025). Embracing strengths and avoiding weaknesses: a meta-analysis of the mnemic neglect effect. Memory, 33(2), 278-294. Abstract read at PubMed; the source for g = 0.365 and its interval.

Kihlstrom, J. F., & Hoyt, I. P. (1990). Repression, Dissociation, and Hypnosis. In J. L. Singer (Ed.), Repression and dissociation, pp. 181-208. Chicago: University of Chicago Press. The first author's posted pre-edit copy read in full and fetched twice; the source for what Clemes did and for the failed replication being described as leaving the evidence equivocal.

Clemes, S. R. (1964). Repression and hypnotic amnesia. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 69(1), 62-69. Crossref and PubMed records only; not read. Crossref gives the author as Stanley Clemens, PubMed as Clemes S.

Stam, H. J., Radtke-Bodorik, H. L., & Spanos, N. P. (1980). Repression and hypnotic amnesia: A failure to replicate and an alternative formulation. Journal of Abnormal Psychology, 89(4), 551-559. Crossref and PubMed records only; not read.

Hilgard, E. R., & Hommel, L. S. (1961). Selective amnesia for events within hypnosis in relation to repression. Journal of Personality, 29(2), 205-216. Crossref record and title only; not read. Cited as the earliest dated use of the phrase this search located.

Cima, M., Merckelbach, H., Hollnack, S., & Knauer, E. (2003). Characteristics of psychiatric prison inmates who claim amnesia. Personality and Individual Differences, 35(2), 373-380. Citation verified at Crossref; not obtained. The 72 of 308 figure is quoted through Mangiulli and colleagues' description of this study.

Otgaar, H., Howe, M. L., Patihis, L., Mangiulli, I., Dodier, O., Huntjens, R., Krackow, E., Jelicic, M., & Lynn, S. J. (2025). The neuroscience of dissociative amnesia and repressed memory: Premature conclusions and unanswered questions. Legal and Criminological Psychology, 30(S1), 29-46. Crossref record and title only; Wiley returned 403.

Markowitsch, H. J., & Staniloiu, A. (2025). Comments. Legal and Criminological Psychology, 30(S1), 46-48. Crossref record and title only; Wiley returned 403. Cited as evidence that the dispute is continuing, not for its contents.

Scheerer, M., & Goldstein, G. (1966). Denial and selective amnesia following brain damage: A case study. Neuropsychologia, 4(4), 357-363. Crossref record and title only; not read. One of the papers the Wikipedia article rests on.

Wikipedia, 'Selective amnesia', wikitext read on 10 August 2026. Used to find the papers named above, and cited as the object of the first problem described in misreadings, not as evidence for anything.
